readerTitle: Why 'too many of you are late' makes more people late
caseNote: 가상 사례 (대기업 재무팀, 포장 공장, 냉동 물류 창고) + 실제 연구 (Petrified Forest 표지판, 영국 국세청 납세 독촉장, 가정 에너지 사용 비교)
insight: "많은 사람이 안 한다"는 경고는 문제를 알리는 말이 아니라 그 행동이 정상이라고 알리는 말이 된다. 사람들이 따라 하길 바라는 행동을 다수의 모습으로 보여줘야 한다.
misconception: 문제가 얼마나 심각한지 숫자로 강조하면 사람들이 경각심을 갖고 행동을 바꾼다.

sources.text: Cialdini, R. B. (1984). Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion.
Cialdini, R. B. et al. (2006). Managing social norms for persuasive impact. Social Influence, 1(1).
Hallsworth, M., List, J., Metcalfe, R., & Vlaev, I. (2017). The behavioralist as tax collector. Journal of Public Economics, 148.
Schultz, P. W. et al. (2007). The constructive, destructive, and reconstructive power of social norms. Psychological Science, 18(5).

factChecks.note: Petrified Forest 연구: '과거 많은 방문객이 나무 화석을 가져갔다'는 표지판이 단순히 가져가지 말라는 표지판보다 도난을 더 늘렸다는 결론을 원문(Cialdini et al., 2006)으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 구체적 비율을 쓰지 않았습니다.
영국 국세청(HMRC) 독촉장 실험: '대부분의 사람이 기한 내 납부한다'는 문구가 납부율을 높였다는 결론을 Hallsworth et al.(2017)로 확인하세요. 카드에는 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다.
Schultz et al.(2007): 평균보다 적게 쓰던 가정이 평균을 알고 나서 사용량을 늘렸고, 칭찬 표시(웃는 얼굴)를 더하자 그 반등이 사라졌다는 내용을 원문으로 확인하세요.
Cialdini가 'social proof'라는 용어를 Influence(1984)에서 널리 알렸다는 표현을 확인하세요. 재무팀·공장·창고 사례와 그 결과는 모두 가상입니다.

cards.title: Why 'too many of you are late' makes more people late
body: A finance team and a packaging plant had the same problem: people skipping a rule they knew about.
The finance team wrote, *"Too many of you are late."* The plant manager wrote, *"Most of you already do this."* Both were true. Only one of them moved people in the right direction.

image.label: Two notices side by side: one warning, one showing a majority
image.brief: 사무실 게시판과 공장 게시판이 나란히 있는 장면. 왼쪽 메모는 빨간 경고 느낌의 "Too many of you are late", 오른쪽 포스터는 초록색 막대와 "Most of this shift wears safety glasses". 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Expense reports keep coming in late.
body: You run finance at a large company. About 40% of expense reports arrive after the deadline, which delays month-end close. You're writing a reminder to all staff.

options.text: "40% of reports were late last month. This has to stop."
options.feedback: It shows how big the problem is, but it also tells the late group they have plenty of company. Being late starts to look normal.

options.text: "6 in 10 colleagues filed on time last month. Join them by Friday."
options.feedback: Same facts, different spotlight. You make filing on time look like what most people do. You give up the alarm, but you gain a model people can follow.

options.text: "Late reports delay everyone's reimbursement. Please file by Friday."
options.feedback: A clear reason helps and does no harm. But it leaves out the strong signal of what everyone else is doing.

cards.title: Same problem, opposite messages.
body: The finance team sent option A. The next month, late reports didn't fall. Some staff took the email as permission: *if nearly half are late, it's not a big deal.*

At the packaging plant, a supervisor noticed people skipping safety glasses. Instead of a warning poster, he ran spot checks and posted the share of workers wearing glasses, by shift, every week. Most were. Over the next weeks, the number crept up as shifts tried to match the best one.

image.label: Weekly chart on a factory wall comparing shifts
image.brief: 공장 휴게실 벽의 주간 차트. 근무조 A, B, C의 보안경 착용률 막대가 매주 조금씩 올라가는 모습. 작업자 두 명이 차트를 보며 이야기하는 장면. 실제 기업 로고 없음.

cards.title: Social proof
body: **Social proof** is our habit of deciding what to do by watching what other people do, especially when we're unsure. The psychologist Robert Cialdini made the term widely known in his 1984 book *Influence*.

The twist is that it works whichever way you point it. A message about a common bad habit spreads the bad habit. The plant pointed people toward the behavior it wanted. The finance team pointed them away from it.

image.label: Arrows from a crowd pointing two ways
image.brief: 가운데 망설이는 사람 한 명, 주변에 여러 사람이 같은 방향으로 걸어가는 단순한 일러스트. 같은 그림을 두 번 그려서 한쪽은 군중이 좋은 행동 쪽으로, 다른 쪽은 나쁜 행동 쪽으로 가는 대비.

cards.title: A sign that increased theft.
body: Cialdini and colleagues tested signs at Petrified Forest National Park, where visitors take pieces of fossilized wood. A sign stressing that *many past visitors had taken wood* led to more theft than a sign that simply asked people not to take it.
The reverse works too. The UK tax authority tested reminder letters saying that most people pay their tax on time. People who got that line paid more promptly than those who got a standard letter.

cards.title: The crowd works best when it looks like you.
body: "Most people" is good. **"Most people like you"** is often stronger. The tax letters were more effective when they pointed to people in the reader's own area. On the shop floor, your own shift beats the whole company.
Uncertainty matters too. People lean on the crowd most when they don't know the right answer, such as a first-time buyer or a new hire.
cards.softwareNote: "Used by 10,000 teams" is weaker than "Used by 300 dental clinics" when the visitor runs a dental clinic. Sorting reviews and case studies by customer type is social proof with the similarity built in.

cards.title: The average pulls both ways.
body: In one energy study, households told they used more power than their neighbors cut back. But households already below average *increased* their use toward the norm. Adding a small sign of approval, a smiley face, stopped that rebound.
So show the norm, then praise people who beat it. And the crowd has to be real. Fake reviews or inflated numbers break trust when they're found out, and in many places they break the law.

cards.title: Now it's a cold-storage warehouse.
body: You run a regional cold-storage and logistics company. Your buyers are food producers nervous about trusting a new partner with frozen goods.
What should your sales page lead with?

options.feedback: A big number helps, but it's vague. A frozen-fish producer can't tell if any of those 500 face their risks.

options.text: Short quotes from three local food producers, with their product type and how long they've used you
options.feedback: Fewer names, but they look like the buyer and speak to the buyer's real fear. You trade scale for similarity, and similarity usually wins here.

options.text: "Many producers worry their goods will spoil in transit"
options.feedback: It names a real fear, but it makes spoilage sound common. You've given social proof to the worry instead of to your service.

cards.title: Show people the crowd doing the right thing.
body: People copy what they believe is normal. So describe the behavior you want as what most people, ideally people like them, already do.
**Try it today:** find one reminder, sign or sales line that warns how many people get it wrong. Rewrite it to show how many get it right.
